text: Alderney Health Systems is a fictional healthcare analytics company with one non-negotiable rule from compliance: patient health information can never leave their own data center or cross a public network. But their fraud-pattern analysis is bursty, heavy compute -- exactly the kind of work that's wasteful to keep provisioned on-prem year-round. This lab designs one coherent architecture that honors both facts at once, instead of picking one and ignoring the other.

The design happens in order, and the order matters. First, classify the data -- raw claims records with identifiers are regulated and immovable; a de-identified, hashed, aggregated extract is portable. Second, design identity before any infrastructure -- one conditional access policy, covering both the on-prem database and the cloud side. Third, design the network path so there's structurally no route for raw data to leak. Fourth, scope the cloud burst job to touch only what already crossed that boundary.

Following the hybrid identity pattern from Chapter four, Alderney extends its on-prem Active Directory into Azure AD, so the same engineers and service accounts authenticate identically on both sides. One conditional access policy, covering both the claims database and the cloud subscription, requires a compliant device and multi-factor authentication, and blocks any access from outside the company's known IP ranges. There's no separate, weaker rule for the cloud side -- the same identity, the same enforcement, everywhere.

The network design has exactly one job: make it structurally impossible for raw claims data to ever reach the cloud. Alderney connects to Azure over a private ExpressRoute circuit, never the public internet, and the de-identified extract lands in a storage account with public network access completely disabled, reachable only through a private endpoint on that same path. The boundary is enforced by the network itself, not by a policy someone has to remember to follow.

The cloud burst job, an AKS cluster that scales up only during the quarterly analysis window, reads exclusively from that de-identified extract and writes its findings back the same way. Nothing identifiable ever has a path to reach it. And the whole design closes with something a compliance reviewer, not just another architect, can actually verify: four plain sentences covering what crosses the boundary, what enforces that, who can access either side, and where the regulated data never moves from.

Lesson twenty-nine proved a regulated workload can be split deliberately between on-prem and cloud, with identity and network boundaries doing the real enforcement. Lesson thirty takes a different kind of portability challenge -- not keeping data in one place, but deploying the exact same Kubernetes workload identically to two different clouds, reusing the multi-cloud Terraform modules this course built back in Chapter three.
